Front matter

How to read this book

It is a specification with a worked implementation attached, which means there are four sensible routes through it and only one of them is cover to cover.

The book is about one question: how do you give a language model the ability to act on a brokerage account without eventually regretting it? Everything here is an answer to some part of that. The descriptor is how you tell the model what a tool does. The ontology is how you stop fourteen descriptors drifting apart. The registry and the runtime are how you make a confident wrong answer harmless. The harness is how you find out whether any of it worked before a customer does.

Four routes

If you areRead
Writing your first tool next week Chapter 4 for the shape of a descriptor, chapter 6 for the description, chapter 15 for one tool built end to end, then chapter 21 for what has to happen around it. About forty pages, and enough to ship something defensible.
Reviewing somebody else's catalog Appendix D is the checklist. Chapter 35 is how to run the meeting. Chapters 9 and 10 are what the governance block has to say, and chapter 37 is the list of things that have actually gone wrong for other people.
Responsible for the platform Parts III, V and VII — the ontology, the registry and the runtime, and the testing. These are the three investments that stop a catalog decaying as it grows, and all three are cheaper to make at ten tools than at sixty.
Here for the agent Part VI. Chapter 25 is what a model is actually reading when it chooses; chapter 27 walks five real conversations tool by tool, including two where the agent is wrong and one where it is right to refuse.

What is in the repository

The companion repository is a working system, not a set of snippets: fourteen conformant descriptors, a brokerage behind them, a registry, a ten-step invocation pipeline, a Spring AI agent over Claude, an Angular console, a desktop connector and an evaluation harness with thirty scenarios. It builds and tests in about fifteen seconds with no API key and no network.

How the code in these pages got here

Every code figure in this book is an excerpt pulled from a file in the repository at build time, by a directive that names the file and the first and last lines to take. Every figure that shows output — an envelope, an error, a confirmation dialog, the generated system prompt, the conformance report, a run of the harness — was recorded from the running system by a capture script and read from disk by the same build.

Nothing is retyped, and that is not a flourish. A specification book whose examples have drifted from its reference implementation is worse than no book, because the reader cannot tell which half to trust. Here, a figure that disagrees with the code is a build failure.

A note on what this book does not cover. It names no wire protocol. The descriptor is a JSON document and publishing it to a particular tool-calling runtime is an adapter — the repository has two, and each is one class. Everything that matters about a tool is in the contract, which is why the contract is what gets specified, linted, reviewed, versioned and tested.

Front matter

The running example

One customer, four accounts, and a book of business arranged so that the easy design decisions fail on it.

Every example in this book runs against the same demonstration customer. The accounts are deliberately awkward, because a catalog tested against a single healthy margin account will do the wrong thing on three accounts out of four and nobody will notice until a customer calls.

Four accounts, and each one breaks something. The margin account can borrow and sell short, so its buying power is not its cash. The cash account can do neither, and its buying power is capped by settled cash, which is a different number again. The Roth IRA cannot sell short at all, and inside it every sentence about holding periods and wash sales is irrelevant. The rollover IRA is frozen, which means an agent that helpfully tries the customer's other account has just done something nobody asked for.

What is in the margin account

Five holdings, one of them an index fund that is 31 percent of the account — concentrated by the numbers and not by any sensible reading, which is the sort of thing an agent should say out loud rather than flag mechanically. Two holdings sit just under the 25 percent line. One, GME, is down a third and is not marginable, so buying more of it needs settled cash even here.

And the money

This is the single most instructive payload in the book. A customer asking “how much have I got?” means one of four things and never says which. cash is the ledger figure. settledCash is what can be spent today without risking a good-faith violation. buyingPower is what can actually be spent on a purchase right now, net of the margin loan and of the cashReservedForOrders already committed to working orders. totalEquity is what the statement will say.

They differ here by a factor of three. A tool that returned one number called balance would be correct a quarter of the time, and the three quarters where it is wrong include every question that ends in somebody spending money.

The conversation this book is about

“Can you sell some of my Apple and put it into the index fund? Actually — how much would that even cost me in tax? And don't do anything in the retirement one.”

Four accounts to choose between, two companies whose names contain the word Apple, a holding split across a long-term lot and a short-term lot bought six weeks ago, a question about tax that must be answered with facts and not advice, and an instruction to stay out of an account that is frozen anyway. Everything in the next four hundred pages exists so that an agent handles that sentence the way a good human would: by asking two questions, showing its arithmetic, and not trading until somebody says yes.

Part I

Foundations

What changes when the caller is a language model, where the trust boundary actually runs, and what the five components of a tool system are each responsible for.

1 What a tool is  ·  2 The five components  ·  3 Conformance levels
Chapter 1

What a tool is

A tool is not an endpoint with a description attached. The difference is the caller, and the caller changes almost everything.

Here is the sentence that most teams start from: we already have a REST API, so we will expose it as tools. It is a reasonable instinct and it produces a catalog that works in a demonstration and disappoints in production. The reason is worth being precise about, because it is not that language models are unreliable. It is that an API and a tool are contracts with different parties, and almost every property an API contract leaves to convention, a tool contract has to state.

Five differences that matter

 An API endpointA tool
The caller A developer who read the documentation once, wrote code, and now calls it the same way forever. Mistakes are found at compile time or in a test. A model that re-reads the description on every turn and decides fresh each time. Mistakes are found in a conversation, by a customer.
Discovery Out of band. The developer browses the docs, picks the endpoint, and nothing in the API itself has to help them choose. In band. Choosing which tool is the hard part, and the only thing that helps is the prose in the description — which is therefore the most load-bearing field.
Arguments Constructed by code from typed values. A malformed request is a bug in the client, and there is one client. Generated from a conversation that may contain anything the customer typed. The schema is the only thing standing between that and your handler.
Errors A status code and a body. The client decides what to do about it, once, in code that was reviewed. Something the model has to read and act on in the moment. A bare 403 teaches it to try the next tool; a sentence teaches it to stop.
Retries Deliberate, bounded, and configured by the client's author. Enthusiastic. A model that reads an error as transient will try again politely for as many turns as it has, and the only thing that stops it is the error saying not to.
An API is read once by a person and then called forever by a program. A tool is read on every single call by something that is reasoning about it afresh.

What follows from that

Four consequences run through the rest of this book, and it is worth meeting them now.

The description is not documentation

In an API, the description is a courtesy. In a tool, it is the decision procedure. When an agent picks the wrong tool, the cause is almost never that the model is incapable; it is that two descriptions did not distinguish themselves, or that one of them failed to say when not to use it. Chapter 6 spends its whole length on this one field, which is the right proportion.

The schema is a boundary, not a type signature

A model follows a closed object schema with narrow patterns very reliably. “Very reliably” is a probability, and the right standard for an order ticket is not a probability. So the schema exists to be enforced at the boundary, every call, before a handler sees an argument — and when it fails, the failure has to name the field, because the caller is going to try again and should try again correctly.

Failures are data

A tool that throws gives the runtime a stack trace and gives the model a wall of text it was never taught to read. A tool that returns ok: false with a code from a closed set gives the model something to branch on and gives the agent's author something to assert in a test. Every tool in this book returns the same envelope whether it succeeded or not; chapter 8 is about that envelope and the fifteen codes inside it.

Some things cannot be left to the model's judgment

The model is a participant in the conversation, and the conversation contains whatever the customer typed. So identity is never an argument. Approval is never a boolean the model sets. The authority to place an order is a single-use token that only a read-only pricing tool can mint. None of this is distrust of the model; it is the same reason a bank teller cannot approve their own withdrawal.

The one-sentence test. If a property of your tool is enforced only by the model choosing to respect it, it is not enforced. Write it down, then ask what in the runtime makes it true. If the answer is “the description asks nicely”, you have a convention, not a control.

What a tool is, then

A tool is a contract with four parts, three audiences and one promise.

Definition

A tool is a named, independently invocable capability, described well enough that a language model can decide when to use it, constrained well enough that the firm can let it, and governed well enough that somebody can be held responsible for it afterwards.

  • For the model: a name, a description and an input schema.
  • For the runtime: an output schema and four behavioral annotations.
  • For the firm: a governance block that never reaches the model at all.

That is the whole of chapter 4, and the next three hundred pages are what each part has to contain, why, and what goes wrong when it does not.

Chapter 2

The five components

Five things, one boundary, and a rule about which side each decision is made on.

Every tool system has the same five parts, whether or not anyone named them. Naming them is useful because the most expensive mistakes are all mistakes about which component owns a decision.

The model
Reads the catalog, decides which tool to call and with what arguments, reads what comes back, and decides again. It is on the untrusted side of the boundary, which is not a judgment about its competence — it is a statement about where its inputs come from.
The runtime
Everything that happens between the model emitting a call and a handler running: resolving the name, validating the arguments, establishing who the call is for, checking entitlements, applying the rate limit, consulting the approval gate, wrapping the result and writing the audit record. This is where the controls live, because it is the first component on the trusted side.
The registry
The one place that knows what tools exist, what each one promises, who may call it and what code is behind it. Without one, the catalog is whatever happened to be on the classpath, and four questions become unanswerable: what is the model being shown, who may call these, which have been reviewed, and what breaks if we turn one off.
The handler
The domain code behind one tool. In a well-built catalog it is startlingly short, because everything generic happens around it. If a handler is long, the tool is usually doing two things.
The system of record
The brokerage itself: the ledger, the order management system, the risk engine, the market data feed. It does not know a model exists and must not have to. Every rule it enforces for a human caller it enforces identically here.

Where the boundary runs

The trust boundary is between the model and the runtime, and it is worth saying plainly what that means, because it is routinely drawn in the wrong place.

It does not mean the model is adversarial. It means that everything the model emits is derived from a conversation, and a conversation contains text that arrived from outside the firm. A customer can type an account identifier that is not theirs. A document the customer pasted can contain a sentence addressed to the model. An email the agent was asked to summarize can say “ignore your previous instructions”. None of that is the model failing; it is the model doing its job on an input it has no way to vet.

So the rule is mechanical:

The boundary rule

A decision may be made on the model's side of the boundary only if a wrong answer is recoverable by the firm's own side. Everything else — identity, entitlement, approval, limits, idempotency — is decided by the runtime, from state the model cannot reach.

Applied to this book's catalog, that is a short and specific list.

DecisionDecided byWhy
which tool to callthe model A wrong choice is refused, costs a turn, and nothing happens.
which accountthe model It can only choose between accounts the customer holds; the handler checks.
how many sharesthe model The risk engine prices it, the customer sees the number, and a human agrees.
who the customer isthe runtime A customer identifier the model can set is an account anyone can read.
what scopes are heldthe runtime A scope the caller can name is not a scope.
whether a human agreedthe runtime A boolean the model sets is a boolean the model will eventually set.
the idempotency keythe runtime A model asked for a unique key will reuse one, or invent a new one on a retry.
how often it may callthe runtime The failure mode being guarded against is a loop, and a loop will not self-limit.

The anatomy of one invocation

Here is a single call, end to end, with the component responsible for each step. Chapter 21 implements it; this is the shape to keep in mind until then.

  1. The model emits a call. A name and a JSON object. Nothing more. It has no session, no identity and no way to set one.
  2. The runtime resolves the name against the registry's view for this principal. A tool this session cannot use is not merely refused; it was never published.
  3. The runtime validates the arguments against the descriptor's input schema. A failure names the field, because the model is about to try again.
  4. The runtime establishes the principal from the session — never from the arguments — and checks every entitlement the descriptor requires.
  5. The runtime applies the rate limit for this principal and this tool.
  6. The runtime consults the approval gate. For a tier 2 or 3 tool with no live grant, the call stops here and the customer is shown what they are being asked to agree to.
  7. The handler runs. It sees a descriptor, validated arguments and a principal. It does not see the conversation, which is why it cannot be talked into anything.
  8. The handler calls the system of record, which applies every rule it would apply to any other caller.
  9. The runtime validates the payload against the descriptor's own output schema and fails closed if it has drifted.
  10. The runtime wraps and records. One envelope, with provenance; one audit record, with field names and never values.

Steps 6 and 9 are the ones people leave out. Chapter 21 argues for both at length. The short version: an approval the model can grant is not an approval, and an output schema nobody enforces is a document the firm published and then stopped honoring.

Chapter 3

Conformance levels

Four levels, so that “is this tool ready?” has an answer shorter than a meeting.

A specification with no levels gets applied unevenly, because the first team to hit a deadline discovers that most of it is optional in practice. Levels fix that by making the exemption explicit: a tool is allowed to be L1, it is simply not allowed to be L1 and also place orders.

LevelMeansRequires
L0 Draft
Not published		 A name and something resembling a description. Fine for an experiment on a branch. An L0 tool may not be served to a model by the registry, which refuses to start with one in an active catalog.
L1 Structurally conformant
Read-only, internal		 All eight fields present. Name matches the grammar. Both schemas are closed objects inside the profile, with a description on every property. All four annotations stated. A governance block with an owner, an entitlement, an audit event and a retention. Passes the linter with no errors.
L2 Contract tested
Customer-facing reads		 Everything in L1, plus: the description follows the seven-part template; every identifier parameter carries the ontology's pattern; the handler has contract tests covering the claims the description makes; the result envelope is enforced; the tool appears in a named evaluation suite and its selection accuracy is recorded.
L3 Certified
Anything that changes state		 Everything in L2, plus: a risk tier agreed at review rather than asserted by the author; an approval mode with a confirmation template that shows the customer the priced consequence; a named kill switch; a refusal suite; a trajectory suite; dual sign-off on the descriptor; and re-certification each quarter against the live catalog.

The rule that makes levels bite

TS-GOV-08 · TS-ANN-04

An active tool must be at least L1. A tool at risk tier 2 or above must be L3 and must require approval. There is no path by which a tool that changes a customer's position reaches a model without a human having signed the descriptor and a human being asked at the moment it runs.

In this book's catalog that works out as ten tools at L2 and four at L3. The four are the preview, which is read-only but mints authority, and the three that change something.

Zero errors and zero warnings is not a boast; it is the only state the build permits. The registry refuses to start on any error, so a non-conformant descriptor physically cannot reach a model. Chapter 31 shows the gate, and Appendix C lists every rule it enforces.

What each level actually buys

Levels are easy to treat as bureaucracy, so it is worth being concrete about what each one prevents.

  • L1 prevents the catalog from becoming inconsistent. Fourteen tools named four different ways is a catalog the model cannot generalize over; it has to learn each one separately, and it will get some of them wrong.
  • L2 prevents the descriptions from being wrong. A contract test asserts the claims the prose makes — that buying power is net of reserved cash, that positions come back largest first, that a lot knows its holding period. Without them the description is a wish.
  • L3 prevents the interesting kind of incident. Not a crash: a correct-looking order, placed confidently, that nobody agreed to. The controls that stop it — the token, the gate, the kill switch, the refusal suite — are exactly the L3 requirements.

A practical note. Do not try to start at L3. Start by getting every read tool to L2 with a linter in CI, which takes about a week and removes most of the inconsistency. Then take the first state-changing tool to L3 properly, once, and copy it. Chapter 38 lays out a first year on that basis.

Part II

The descriptor

Eight fields. Four of them decide what the model does, one is a promise to the caller, and three never reach the model at all. This part is what each one has to contain and what goes wrong when it does not.

4 The eight fields  ·  5 Names  ·  6 The description is the contract  ·  7 Schemas and the profile  ·  8 The envelope and the errors  ·  9 Annotations, tiers and approval  ·  10 Governance metadata
Chapter 4

The eight fields

And only eight. Anything else is an implementation detail of whoever happens to be serving it.

A descriptor is a JSON document. That is a design decision rather than a format preference, and it is worth defending before we look at the fields, because the alternative — assembling the descriptor in code, from annotations — is what most teams reach for first.

Why the descriptor is data

There is no @Tool annotation anywhere in this book's repository. Each tool is a file. The consequences are concrete:

  • A reviewer who does not write Java can read it, and a change to a description shows up in a pull request as a diff of prose.
  • A linter can check it, which is how 58 rules become a build step rather than a style guide.
  • A desktop client can be handed it without the application running.
  • You can answer “what exactly is the model being shown right now?” by reading a file, instead of starting a service and inspecting a builder.
  • Publishing to a second runtime is an adapter of about forty lines that renames nothing.

The annotated approach is faster for the first three tools and does not scale past a dozen, because the thing that needs review is prose, and prose inside a Java string literal is prose nobody reviews.

The eight fields, by audience

name
model

The identity the model emits. Permanent. Lowercase, underscores, three segments.

title
model & humans

A short label for an approval dialog or an audit screen. Not a second description.

description
model

The decision procedure. Seven parts. The field the model's choice actually turns on.

inputSchema
model

A closed object inside the profile. Every property described, every string constrained.

outputSchema
caller

A promise about the payload, enforced on the way out so it cannot quietly become false.

annotations
runtime

Four booleans, all stated explicitly, that tell the runtime how much to trust the call.

icons
interfaces

Decorative only. No control anywhere may depend on an icon being present.

_meta
the firm

Governance, under a reverse-DNS key. Never rendered into the model's context.

Here is the record, which is the whole specification expressed as a type.

And here is the smallest conformant descriptor in the catalog, in full. Everything in Part II is an explanation of some part of it.

That figure is the manifest, not the file. It is what the descriptor becomes when it is published to a model: name, description, input schema, and nothing else. The file itself carries five more fields that the model never sees. Appendix F prints all fourteen in full; chapter 15 builds this one from nothing.

What the model actually receives

This is worth internalizing early, because it changes how you write every other field. When the catalog is published, the model's context contains, for each tool, three strings: the name, the description and the serialized input schema. That is all.

It does not contain the output schema. It does not contain the annotations, the risk tier, the owner, the entitlements or the retention period. A model cannot read destructiveHint: true and be careful, because it never sees it. If you want the model to know that a tool cannot be undone, the description has to say so in words.

The context rule

Anything the model must know in order to behave correctly belongs in the description. Anything the runtime must know in order to behave correctly belongs in the annotations or the governance block. Writing a fact in the wrong one of those places is the same as not writing it.

What it costs

The catalog in this book is fourteen tools. Published to a trading session, the names, descriptions and schemas come to about 26,000 characters — on the order of sixty-six hundred tokens — and the generated briefing adds roughly fifteen hundred more. That is a real cost on every single turn, and it is the reason chapter 6 gives the description a budget and chapter 7 gives the schema one.

It is also the reason the catalog is filtered by entitlement before it is published rather than after. A research session sees three tools and pays for three; a read-only desktop session sees ten and pays about fifteen thousand characters.

Chapter 5

Names

A name is the one field you can never change, so it is worth the twenty minutes.

The grammar

TS-NAM-01 · TS-NAM-02

^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,63}$, with the shape <domain>_<entity>_<operation>.

Lowercase and underscores because that is the intersection of what every tool-calling runtime accepts. Three segments because two leave the model guessing which catalog a tool belongs to when a firm has six of them.

The character set is not an aesthetic choice. Runtimes differ on hyphens, on dots, on camelCase, on length and on leading digits, and the differences are discovered at the worst possible time: when you publish an existing catalog somewhere new and a third of it is rejected or, worse, silently renamed. The intersection is small and boring and it travels.

Dots never cross the wire

A catalog wants a hierarchy — brokerage.orders.place reads better than brokerage_orders_place and sorts into a tree. So the descriptor carries both, and they are derived from each other rather than maintained separately.

The dotted form appears in the console, in dashboards and in configuration. The underscore form is what the model emits. Because one is computed from the other, they cannot disagree.

The name is derived, not chosen

This is the part that surprises people, and it is the single highest-leverage idea in Part III. In this catalog nobody picks a tool name. The ontology declares one capability row per tool, and the name falls out of it:

The entity supplies the term, the operation supplies the verb, and the capability's cardinality decides between the singular and the plural form. So brokerage_order_cancel could not have been called cancelOrder, or brokerage_cancel_order, or brokerage_orders_cancel. A linter rule compares the two and fails the build if a descriptor has drifted.

The verb vocabulary is closed

Seven verbs, and a tool may use no others.

VerbRead-only Base tierMeans
listyesT0 The members of a collection, bounded and paged. Needs no identifier it does not already have, which is what makes it a safe first move.
getyesT0 One named entity, or a plain statement that it is not there.
searchyesT0 Free text to candidates. Returns a list to choose between, never a choice.
previewyesT1 Computes exactly what a change would do, changes nothing, and mints the authority to go ahead.
placenoT3 Commits a change the customer has seen and approved.
replacenoT3 Amends a live instruction in place, keeping its identifier.
cancelnoT2 Requests that a live instruction stop, and reports what actually happened to it.

A closed vocabulary pays for itself twice. First, the model generalizes: having learned what list means on one tool, it is right about it on the other four. Second — and this is the part that matters at review time — the annotations and the risk tier can be checked against the name instead of trusted from the descriptor, which is the one place a tool author's optimism is most expensive.

Titles

Three to sixty characters, no trailing period, and unique across the catalog. The title is what a human sees in an approval dialog and in an audit screen, which is the whole of its job.

The rule that caught this book's own test fixture. Two tools may not share a title. A person approving one of two things both called “a fixture tool” cannot tell which they are approving. The first thing the linter found when the pipeline's test fixtures were written was exactly that, in this book's own repository.

Names are permanent

Renaming a tool is a breaking change of an unusual kind: it breaks a model, and nothing compiles differently. Every recorded evaluation references the old name. Every audit record for the last six years references the old name. Any prompt a customer saved references the old name. Chapter 36 covers the deprecation path, which is to publish both for a window and retire one — but the cheaper answer is to spend twenty minutes on the ontology first.

Chapter 6

The description is the contract

This is the field. Everything else in the descriptor constrains what happens after the model has chosen; this is the only field that affects whether it chooses correctly.

When an agent does the wrong thing, there are three candidate causes and they are not equally likely. It is rarely that the model is incapable. It is sometimes that the toolset is missing a tool. It is usually that two descriptions did not distinguish themselves, or that one of them never said when not to use it.

The seven parts

A description is plain prose — no markdown, no bullet lists, no headings — and it covers seven things in roughly this order.

 PartWhat it has to do
1What it does One sentence, naming the fields it returns. Specific enough that the model knows what it will get back without calling it.
2When to use it The situations in the customer's words, not yours. “Use when the customer asks what they can spend”, not “retrieves account balance information”.
3When not to use it And what to use instead, by name. This is the half nobody writes and the half that does the work.
4What has to happen first Which identifiers it needs and where they come from. Redundant with the ontology, and worth repeating because the model reads this and not the ontology.
5What it changes For a read tool, one sentence saying it changes nothing. For anything else, what the change is and whether it can be undone.
6How to read the result Which field to look at first, and what a particular value means. This is where you spend the model's attention well.
7Limits and caveats Staleness, estimates, pagination, anything that makes the answer less than it looks.

A description, annotated

Here is the description of brokerage_quotes_get, which is a tool with nothing clever about it, broken into its seven parts.

1 — what it does. “Returns the current two-sided market for each symbol given: last price, bid, ask, size, change on the day, volume, the spread in basis points, and the session the venue is in.”

2 — when to use it. “Use when the customer asks what something is trading at, asks to compare instruments, or before explaining what an order would cost. Pass every symbol in one call rather than calling once per symbol.”

3 — when not to. “Do not use to look up a company by name — that is brokerage_instruments_search — and do not use it for past prices, which is brokerage_price_history_get.”

6 — how to read it. “Read asOf before quoting a number to the customer: a quote is perishable and one taken minutes ago is not the market now. Read session too, and say so when it is not regular. Read spreadBasisPoints before recommending a market order; above about 25 basis points the fill can be well away from the last price and a limit order is the better advice.”

5 and 7 — effect and caveats. “This changes nothing and may be called freely.”

Four hundred and sixty words of schema and about a hundred and thirty words of prose, and the prose is what makes the model batch the call, warn about a wide spread, and not reach for this tool when the customer said “Apple”.

The budget

TS-DSC-01 · TS-DSC-02

At least 120 characters, at most 2000. Below the floor a description cannot have said when not to use the tool. Above the ceiling it crowds out the conversation and the model starts skimming — and a skimmed description is worse than a short one, because the part it skips is unpredictable.

The fourteen descriptions in this catalog run from 650 to 1,500 characters. The longest is the preview tool, which earns it: it is the only tool whose misuse cannot be undone and the only one that mints authority.

Writing for a model, not about a tool

Five habits, each of which measurably changes behavior.

Use the customer's words

The model is matching against an utterance. “Use when the customer asks what they can spend” matches “how much can I spend?”. “Retrieves account balance information” matches nothing a customer has ever said.

Name the alternative

“Do not use this for X” leaves the model with a prohibition and no plan. “Do not use this for X; that is brokerage_other_tool” moves it somewhere. The linter checks that every tool named in a description exists in the catalog, because a dangling redirection is worse than none — the model will try it.

Say which field to read first

A payload with twelve fields has an order of importance that the JSON does not express. The preview tool's description says “Read canPlace first: false means the order would be refused.” That one sentence is the difference between an agent that relays a blocker and an agent that reports a cost for an order that cannot be placed.

Give the stop condition

Models are helpful, and helpfulness under a refusal looks like trying something else. So the descriptions say so explicitly: “tell the customer rather than retrying”, “do not try another account on their behalf”, “never preview again simply to obtain a fresh token for an order the customer has not re-approved”.

Write the consequence, not the mechanism

Compare “this operation is not idempotent” with “the effect is immediate and cannot be undone: a filled order can only be reversed by trading in the opposite direction, at whatever the market then is, and the customer bears that difference”. The second is longer and it is the one that changes behavior.

What the linter can check

Prose quality is a review matter, but four things about it are mechanical, and mechanical things belong in the build.

Length, the presence of a “when to use” and a “when not to”, markdown, the first person, cross-references that resolve, and — for anything that changes state — whether the description says so. None of that is a substitute for someone reading it. All of it is a substitute for someone having to read it before they can get to the interesting question.

A reviewer should be arguing about whether the description tells the truth. Everything mechanical belongs in the linter.
Chapter 7

Schemas and the profile

JSON Schema is much larger than any tool-calling runtime supports, and the parts supported unevenly are exactly the parts that fail silently.

The failure mode is specific and worth seeing before the rules. You write a schema with oneOf, describing two legitimate shapes of request. A runtime on the way to the model drops the keyword, because its own schema translation does not support it. The model is now shown a schema in which both branches' fields are simply optional. It produces an object matching neither, cheerfully, and the runtime that dropped the keyword has no way to say so. Your handler receives it, and whatever it does next, nobody was warned.

The profile is a whitelist

The rule behind it: a keyword is permitted when it either constrains a scalar in a way every runtime forwards, or describes structure. Keywords that express alternation, negation or conditionals are not, because they are the ones that get dropped.

Prohibited keywords are rejected rather than ignored, and each rejection carries the reason the author needs to hear:

Six rules that do most of the work

Close every object
additionalProperties: false, everywhere, without exception. An open object means the model's invented extra field is silently accepted and silently ignored — and the model has no way to learn that the field did nothing. Closing it turns an invisible misunderstanding into an error that names the field.
Describe every property
The field name is not the contract. quantity could be shares or dollars; price could be a limit or a last trade; since could be a date or a cursor. Where the name is ambiguous the model will pick the common reading, and the common reading is wrong about a third of the time in a brokerage.
Constrain every string
An unconstrained string accepts anything the model invents. Every string in this catalog carries an enum, a pattern, a format, or at minimum a maxLength. A pattern is best, because it is also what stops a malformed identifier reaching the handler.
Money is a decimal string
Never a JSON number. IEEE-754 binary doubles cannot represent 0.1, so a thousand shares at $10.10 totals $10099.999999999998, and the model will read that back to a customer. The linter warns on any number in an input schema for exactly this reason. The pattern this book uses is ^-?[0-9]{1,15}(\.[0-9]{1,6})?$.
Bound every array in an output
maxItems, always. An unbounded array in a result is an unbounded token bill, and it is discovered by a long-standing customer whose four years of fills arrive in one payload on the first turn of a conversation.
Twelve parameters is the practical ceiling
Past about a dozen, a model starts omitting the ones it is least certain about, and the ones it is least certain about are usually the ones you added last because they were subtle. A tool with eighteen parameters is almost always two tools.

Reserved parameter names

Some names a tool may never use, because the runtime has claimed them and a tool that accepts one has created a way around a check somebody wrote on purpose.

Note where the line is drawn. accountId is not reserved, because choosing between the accounts a customer holds is exactly what the model is for. customerId is reserved, because a customer identifier the model can set is an account anyone can read. The distinction is between scope within an established identity and the identity itself.

The ones that look harmless. dryRun, force, skipValidation, override. Each is a flag that turns a control off, settable by the party the control exists to constrain. If a tool genuinely needs both behaviors, that is two tools with two risk tiers and two descriptions — which is precisely what preview and place are.

Validation is not optional

Every invocation is validated against the input schema before a handler sees an argument, and every payload is validated against the output schema before it is returned. The second surprises people, so chapter 21 defends it properly. The short version is that the output schema is the only description of the payload the model will ever see, and a handler that drifts from it is misleading the model with a document the firm published.

When validation fails, the violations are rendered for the model, pointer first, and capped at five — because a model handed twenty violations fixes the first three and re-sends.

Chapter 8

The envelope and the errors

Every tool returns the same shape whether it worked or not, and a failure is something the model reads rather than something it survives.

One envelope

Four fields. ok is the discriminator the model branches on. data is the payload, and it is the thing the descriptor's outputSchema describes. error is present exactly when ok is false. And meta is never optional.

The envelope is specified once, here, rather than repeated inside fourteen output schemas. That is a deliberate trade: the model learns the shape once and carries it across the whole catalog, and the schemas stay about the domain. It does mean the envelope has to be described to the model somewhere, which is one short paragraph of the generated briefing in chapter 26.

Why meta is mandatory

Three of its fields answer questions that come up constantly and that a handler, left to its own judgment, will sometimes omit.

  • asOf is the instant the data describes, not the instant the envelope was written. The moment a quote is involved this is the difference between a number and a misquote.
  • complete says whether the model is looking at everything or at a page. An agent that summarizes page one as though it were the whole is a specific and very common failure, and this field is what prevents it.
  • requestId is the only thing a customer can quote back to support. Every error's remediation tells the agent to give it to them.

Failures are data

A handler says no by throwing a ToolFailure, which the pipeline turns straight into an ok: false envelope. An exception is the handler's convenience — a guard clause reads better than threading a result type through five calls — and the model never sees an exception, a class name or a stack trace.

Nothing else may escape a handler. An unexpected exception is caught by the pipeline, logged with the request identifier, and returned as INTERNAL_ERROR with no detail — because the alternative is leaking a database constraint name into a customer conversation. There is a test for exactly that.

The taxonomy is closed

Fifteen codes, and a tool may return no others. A closed taxonomy exists so that the agent can be taught once what to do about each code instead of inferring it from prose every time.

Each code carries three things: whether an identical retry could plausibly succeed, whether the caller has anything to change, and the sentence the generated briefing shows the model. Keeping the sentence next to the flags it has to agree with is the difference between a prompt that matches the taxonomy and a prompt that used to.

The two flags combine into four behaviors, and every code is one of them.

retryablecallerCanFix The agent shouldCodes
noyesFix the call and try the same tool again INVALID_ARGUMENT, UNKNOWN_TOOL, NOT_FOUND, APPROVAL_REQUIRED, CONFIRMATION_EXPIRED, CONFLICT, AMBIGUOUS_REQUEST
yesnoWait if told how long, then report and stop RATE_LIMITED, UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE, UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT, INTERNAL_ERROR
nonoTell the customer and stop. Nothing else will help NOT_ENTITLED, PRECONDITION_FAILED, QUOTA_EXCEEDED, UNSUPPORTED
neither There is no fourth combination: a code that is both retryable and the caller's to fix would be telling the agent two different things at once, which is how retry loops start.

Three fields that make an error actionable

remediation, in the imperative

Not “the account was not found” but “call brokerage_accounts_list to get the accounts this customer actually holds, and use an accountId from that result”. The imperative is the form an agent follows most reliably, and naming the next tool is what turns a dead end into a step.

retryAfterSeconds

Only on RATE_LIMITED, and always when it appears. “Too many requests” tells an agent to wait and gives it no way to decide how long, which in practice means it waits for zero seconds.

candidates

Only on AMBIGUOUS_REQUEST. The whole point of that code is that the tool refuses to choose, and a refusal without the choices attached makes the agent guess from memory. In this catalog ambiguity is usually surfaced as a successful search returning several candidates rather than as an error — which is a better design where it is available, because an error is a thing to recover from and a list is a thing to ask about.

One mistake worth naming

Do not map upstream status codes straight through. A 404 from the position service and a 404 from the market data service mean different things to an agent: one means the customer does not hold it, the other means the ticker does not exist, and the right next move differs. Map deliberately, at the handler, where you know which upstream it was. Appendix B has the mapping table this catalog uses.

Chapter 9

Annotations, tiers and approval

Four booleans the runtime trusts, four tiers it does not take on faith, and the difference between the two.

The four annotations

AnnotationTrue when
readOnlyHint The tool changes nothing anywhere. Not “nothing the customer can see” — nothing.
destructiveHint A change may be irreversible or may overwrite existing state. A placed order is destructive; a cancellation is not, because it removes exposure rather than creating it.
idempotentHint Repeating the identical call has no additional effect. Read tools get this for free. A write tool earns it, usually with a key.
openWorldHint The tool reaches outside the firm's controlled domain — a market data feed, a venue. It is the field that says “the answer can change without anyone here doing anything”.
TS-ANN-01

All four are stated explicitly on every descriptor, even where the value is the specification's default. “Absent” and “false” are read differently by different runtimes, and a trading tool cannot afford that ambiguity.

Two combinations are contradictions and the linter rejects them: a tool cannot be both read-only and destructive, and a read-only tool is idempotent by construction.

Why the annotations are not enough

The annotations are asserted by the tool's author. They are useful — the runtime uses them to decide what to log and what to show — and they are exactly the wrong thing to hang a control on, because the author is also the person most likely to be optimistic about their own tool.

So the control hangs on the risk tier, which is agreed at review and, in this catalog, derived from the ontology rather than written by hand.

Four tiers

TierMeans ApprovalEvidence required
T0 Reads data
A wrong call costs a turn		 none Conformance lint and handler contract tests.
T1 Reads, and reaches
Risk engines, or mints authority		 none Adds a selection evaluation: the agent must choose it for the utterances it is for, and not for the ones it is not.
T2 Changes state, reduces exposure confirm Adds a trajectory evaluation and a recorded human approval for every invocation.
T3 Changes state, creates exposure confirm Adds dual sign-off on the descriptor, a named kill switch, a refusal suite, and quarterly re-certification against the live catalog.

The tier-1 line is the one that gets argued about, so here is the case. brokerage_order_preview is read-only: it changes nothing a customer can observe, and its description truthfully tells the model to call it as often as it likes while the customer adjusts an order. It is nevertheless not tier 0, because it reaches the risk and margin engines and because it mints a ConfirmationToken, and minting authority is not nothing.

The cancel asymmetry

brokerage_order_cancel is tier 2 where the other two writes are tier 3, and it is the one asymmetry in the catalog worth defending out loud.

Cancelling reduces exposure. Requiring a priced preview before a customer can stop an order would mean that in the one situation where speed matters — a price running away from them — the system is at its slowest. So cancel needs no confirmation token. It still requires the customer's explicit approval at the moment it runs; what it does not need is a round trip through the risk engine to find out what stopping something would cost.

Approval modes

ModeMeans
noneRuns. Everything at tier 0 and 1.
notifyRuns, and somebody is told afterwards. Useful for tools that are safe but surprising.
confirmThe customer is shown what will happen and says yes before it runs. Everything at tier 2 and 3 in this catalog.
dualControlTwo different humans. Reserved here for a notional value above 250,000, an account under review, or any restricted-classification tool.
humanExecutionThe agent prepares it and a human performs it. The honest answer when a capability is too consequential to automate but too useful to omit.

What a confirmation has to show

This is where the design most often goes quietly wrong, so it gets its own rule and its own worked failure.

TS-ANN-05

An approval mode above notify requires a confirmationTemplate, and the rendered template must state the priced consequence — not the tool name, not the arguments, the consequence. A dialog that says “allow this tool?” is not informed consent.

The template for brokerage_order_place wants to say “Estimated cost 10,978.20 USD” and “in Everyday brokerage”. Neither is an argument. The arguments are an account identifier, a ticker, a side and a quantity; the cost does not exist until something prices it, and the nickname lives in the account record. Render the template from the arguments alone and the customer sees this:

A customer will approve that, because the part they recognize is correct. They will have approved an order whose cost they never saw. The fix is an ApprovalContext: the runtime asks the domain for the figures the arguments do not carry, at the moment of the confirmation.

With it, the same call produces the dialog the customer should see — and the figures are computed now, not carried forward from a preview that may be a minute old.

Chapter 22 implements the gate behind it, and chapter 17 explains why the token and the approval are two separate mechanisms rather than one.

Chapter 10

Governance metadata

The part of the descriptor the model never sees, and the part somebody will be reading in an incident review two years from now.

Governance lives in _meta, under a reverse-DNS key, so that it travels with the descriptor and is never rendered into the model's context. Every field in it answers a question that gets asked eventually.

Field by field

version
Semantic, and it versions the contract rather than the implementation. A handler fix is a patch. A new optional parameter is a minor. Narrowing a pattern, renaming an output field or removing an enum value is a major — see chapter 36, because the list of what breaks a model is not the list that breaks a compiler.
lifecycle
draft, active, deprecated, retired. The registry serves only active, however complete a draft looks.
conformanceLevel & riskTier
Asserted by the owner, verified at review. In this catalog the tier is checked against the ontology on every build, so an author cannot quietly demote a tool to avoid an approval requirement.
owner
A team, a mailbox and a paging escalation. All three, because at two in the morning a mailbox is not a person. An unowned tool in production is an incident waiting for a volunteer.
dataClassification & piiFields
The highest classification the tool can return, and JSON pointers to any personal data in the output. Pointers rather than a boolean, because masking and retention are mechanical and need to know where to look. The linter rejects containsPii: true with an empty pointer list.
entitlements
Scopes the principal must hold, all of them. This is the field the registry filters on, so a tool with no entitlement is a tool anybody can call — which the linter treats as an error rather than a default.
approval
The mode, the confirmation template, and an expiry. An approval with no window is a standing instruction, and nobody means to give one of those.
recordKeeping
An audit event name, an ISO 8601 retention, and the obligations driving it. In this catalog the trading tools are P6Y against books-and-records and order audit trail; the tax lot tool is P7Y; market data is P2Y and is driven by licensing rather than by regulation.
cost & rateLimit
A cost class, a p95 latency and a per-principal budget. The limits that matter differ by two orders of magnitude — 180 quote calls a minute is normal, 180 order placements a minute is an incident — which is why the limit is per tool and not per catalog.
dependencies & availability
What it calls, its SLO, and a named kill switch. Every tool at tier 2 or above must name one, because when a tool starts behaving badly the options are to turn it off or to roll back, and only one of those takes less than a build.
evaluation
The suite that measures whether the model picks this tool correctly, when it last ran, and what it scored. A tier 2 or 3 tool that cites no suite does not pass the linter. This is what makes the number an assertion somebody can check rather than a number somebody typed.

A governance block, in full

The JSON spellings are pinned

One detail that looks fussy and is not. The enumerations in the governance block declare their wire spellings explicitly rather than deriving them from the Java constant names.

These strings appear in published descriptors and in audit records with six-year retentions. Renaming a Java constant must never silently change a wire value, and the only way to guarantee that is to write the wire value down.

The same argument applies to one enumeration in the domain. CANCELLED keeps its double-L spelling throughout this book, in a text that is otherwise US English, because it is the spelling in the systems of record the domain borrows from. An enumeration member is a name rather than prose, and renaming it to match the surrounding prose would break every consumer already matching on the string.

Part III

The ontology

What a catalog is supposed to cover, written down once, so that names, risk tiers and prerequisites are derived rather than argued about. The investment that stops a catalog decaying as it grows.

11 Why a catalog needs one  ·  12 Entities, operations, capabilities  ·  13 The producer graph  ·  14 Conformance against the ontology
Chapter 11

Why a catalog needs an ontology

It sounds like an academic luxury until the catalog passes about a dozen tools. Then three problems arrive at once.

Nobody designs a tool catalog badly on purpose. What happens is that the first five tools are written by one person in a week, the next fifteen by four people over a quarter, and the forty after that by teams who have read the first twenty and drawn their own conclusions. By then the catalog has three diseases, and they are not independent.

The three problems

One: the names stop agreeing

Here is a real-shaped catalog after a year without an ontology.

The cost is not aesthetic. A model that has learned what _list means on one tool generalizes it to the next, and a catalog with four naming schemes forces it to learn each tool separately. Selection accuracy degrades gradually and nobody can point at the change that caused it, because there wasn't one.

Two: nobody can say whether the catalog is complete

“Do we cover everything a customer might ask about their account?” is a reasonable question from a product owner and an unanswerable one without a statement of what the catalog ought to cover. In practice the answer is somebody's memory of what has been built, which is how a firm ends up with four ways to read an order and no way to read an execution.

Three: the risk tiers become a matter of taste

This is the expensive one. Each descriptor asserts its own tier. The author of the cancellation tool thinks tier 2; the author of the replacement tool thinks tier 1, because “it's only an amendment”; and two years later an auditor asks why one tool that changes a customer's exposure needs an approval and another does not. There is no good answer, because the two decisions were made in different weeks by different people with no shared rule.

An ontology is not documentation about the catalog. It is the thing the catalog is generated and checked against.

What an ontology fixes, mechanically

All three, and it fixes them by moving decisions from the descriptor to one reviewed file.

Instead ofThe ontology gives you
Choosing a name A name derived from the entity and the operation. A descriptor whose name does not match what the ontology derives fails the build (TS-ONT-02).
Asserting a risk tier A tier that comes from the operation, with every exception recorded as an override and a note that a reviewer reads (TS-ONT-05).
Asserting an approval mode A mode that follows from the tier by a policy table edited in one place (TS-ONT-06).
Hoping the entitlements are right An entitlement floor per entity, so a tool that reads orders cannot be published without the orders scope (TS-ONT-07).
Copying a regex between schemas Identifier types declared once, and a check that every parameter consuming one carries its pattern character for character (TS-ONT-09).
Guessing what the agent needs first A producer graph: which tool hands out each identifier, and therefore what has to happen before what. Chapter 13.
Asking whether the catalog is complete A capability table. Completeness becomes a question about rows rather than about memory, and a declared capability with no descriptor fails the build (TS-SET-02).

The cost

It is one file of about three hundred lines for this catalog, and an afternoon to write the first version. The honest objection is not the cost but the timing: at three tools an ontology is overhead, and at sixty it is a migration. The right moment is somewhere around ten, which is also the moment nobody has time for it.

A cheap way to start. Write the capability table first and nothing else — one row per tool, with the operation, the entity and the identifiers it consumes and produces. That table alone gives you the naming rule, the completeness question and the producer graph. The entities, the policies and the identifier types can follow in a second pass, and each one turns another review argument into a build step.

Chapter 12

Entities, operations, capabilities

Building the brokerage ontology, one decision at a time, with the arguments.

The ontology has five sections and they are worth meeting in the order you would write them: the identifier types that join calls together, the entities the domain is about, the operations that may be performed, the capabilities that pair them, and the policies that follow.

Identifier types

Start here, because identifiers are what make a multi-step conversation possible and what make it go wrong.

Three properties, each load-bearing.

They are prefixed. acct_ can never be mistaken for ord_, which means a misrouted identifier fails at the schema rather than in the handler, and the error names the field.

They are opaque, and the ontology says so. Nothing downstream may parse an account identifier for a branch code or an open date, because the day somebody does is the day the format can never change. The opaque flag is what the generated briefing uses to tell the model which identifiers it must never construct.

Their patterns are declared once. This is the one that catches real bugs. Look at the symbol pattern:

^[A-Z]{1,5}(\.[A-Z])?$

The optional dot-suffix is the whole point. A pattern of ^[A-Z]{1,5}$ looks right, passes every test anyone writes, and silently rejects BRK.B — which is how a customer discovers that your agent cannot price Berkshire Hathaway. Declaring the pattern once means fourteen descriptors cannot each get it wrong in their own way.

Entities

An entity is a thing the domain is about. Each one carries the slugs that appear in tool names, the identifier that addresses it, the classification floor and the entitlement floor for any tool that touches it, and its relations to other entities.

The brokerage ontology declares nine. Three decisions in that list are worth defending.

Balances is an entity, not a field on Account

The money view has its own entity because it has its own entitlement (brokerage:balances:read), its own freshness and its own tool. A service session that may list accounts does not automatically see what is in them; in a firm with a support desk that distinction is the difference between a reasonable permission and an unreasonable one.

TaxLot is an entity, not a detail of Position

Because selling is a choice between lots and the choice is worth money. Modeling lots as a nested array inside the position payload would have meant that every “what do I own?” question paid for a tax breakdown nobody asked for, and that a conversation about tax could not happen without one about market value.

Order is the only mutable entity

"mutable": true appears exactly once in this ontology, and everything expensive about the catalog is downstream of that sentence. Four tools touch it, three of them change it, all three are tier 2 or above, and the whole of chapter 17 exists because of it.

Operations

A closed vocabulary of seven verbs, each declaring whether it is read-only, whether it is idempotent, and what risk tier it starts from.

The semantics field is prose for humans and it is where the real design lives. “Never requires an identifier the agent does not already hold, which is what makes a list tool a safe first move” is a design rule, and writing it next to the verb means the next person adding a list tool reads it.

Capabilities

A capability is one row: this tool is this operation on this entity, it needs these identifiers and it hands back those. The table is the catalog's specification; the descriptors implement it.

Here are three rows from the brokerage table, chosen because each makes a different point.

That last row is how an exception is supposed to look. cancel has a base tier of 2 while its siblings have 3, and the note says why in a sentence a reviewer can disagree with. An exception with no note is a rule somebody quietly opted out of.

Policies

Finally, the rules that turn a tier into an approval mode, and the ceiling on what one agent turn may do without a human.

These live in the ontology rather than in each descriptor so that raising the bar — moving tier 2 from confirm to dualControl, say — is one edit, reviewable in one diff, and checked against every descriptor on the next build.

Chapter 13

The producer graph

The one thing an agent needs that no single descriptor can tell it: where the arguments come from.

A descriptor describes one tool. It can say “accountId, from brokerage_accounts_list” in a property description, and it should. But that sentence is a claim one author made about another author's tool, and nothing checks it. Multiply by fourteen and some of those claims are stale.

The producer graph derives the same facts from the capability table, which means they cannot be stale, and makes them available as a whole rather than one tool at a time.

Two maps

The first says, for each identifier type, which tools hand one out. The second inverts it: for each tool, which tools must have run first because they are the only source of something it needs. Both are computed, not written.

What it says about this catalog

Preview is the only way in

Read the right-hand side again. brokerage_order_place consumes a ConfirmationToken. Exactly one capability in this catalog produces one, and it is the read-only preview. There is no other path.

That is a different kind of guarantee from a description that says “please preview first”. The description does say it, and should. But the reason the agent cannot skip the preview is not that it read the description and complied; it is that the argument does not exist anywhere else. A test asserts the property directly:

Dead ends

The graph also answers a question nobody thinks to ask: is there an identifier some tool needs that nothing in the catalog produces?

Every one is a tool the agent can read about and can never correctly call, because the argument has to come from the customer typing an opaque identifier exactly right. It happens more than you would expect — usually when a tool is ported from an internal API where the caller already had the identifier from somewhere else. The linter makes it a build failure (TS-SET-03).

And it writes the system prompt

The producer graph is not only a diagram. The toolset half of the system prompt is generated from these two maps, so what the picture says and what the model is told cannot disagree. Chapter 26 is about that; here is the paragraph it produces from the graph above.

Chapter 14

Conformance against the ontology

Nine rules that turn a design document into a build step.

An ontology that nothing checks is a diagram on a wiki. These are the rules that make it bind, and each one exists because of a specific way a catalog drifts from its own design.

RuleChecks The drift it catches
TS-ONT-01Every descriptor has a capability A tool built in a hurry that the ontology has never heard of — which usually means it is doing something the domain was not designed to do.
TS-ONT-02The name matches what the ontology derives A rename, a plural that should be singular, a verb in the wrong position.
TS-ONT-03The capability's entity and operation exist A typo in the ontology itself.
TS-ONT-04readOnlyHint agrees with the operation A write tool annotated read-only, which is the single most consequential annotation error available.
TS-ONT-05The risk tier matches the policy A tool quietly demoted to avoid an approval requirement.
TS-ONT-06The approval mode matches the tier A tier 3 tool with mode: none, usually left over from development.
TS-ONT-07The entity's entitlement is held A reader of orders published without the orders scope, visible to every session.
TS-ONT-08The classification is not below the entity's Customer data published as internal, which changes who may see the logs.
TS-ONT-09Every consumed identifier's pattern is carried A looser pattern on one tool than on its neighbors — how a malformed identifier reaches a handler.

Two of them, as code

And the pattern check, which is the one that catches the most bugs per line:

Rules about the set, not the tool

Three more rules look at the catalog as a whole, which is where the interesting gaps are.

TS-SET-01 catches two tools sharing a title. TS-SET-02 catches a capability the ontology declares and nothing implements — which is the completeness question, asked automatically. TS-SET-03 catches the dead ends from chapter 13. And TS-SET-04 warns when most of a catalog changes state, because a model needs reads to orient itself before it is safe to let it write.

It fails at startup, not at call time

The registry runs the linter in its constructor and refuses to build if anything is in error.

A non-conformant descriptor therefore cannot reach a model. Not “should not”; cannot — the application does not start. The same rules also run as an ordinary unit test, which is what fails the build for everyone, and as a command, which gives whoever is writing a descriptor a one-second loop instead of a Maven cycle.

Why both. The test is the gate. The command is the ergonomics. A gate with bad ergonomics gets worked around, and a gate that is worked around is a style guide.

Part IV

Building the catalog

Fourteen tools, built in the order you would build them: the entry point first, then the reads that make a conversation possible, then the four that can change a customer's position.

15 The first tool, end to end  ·  16 The nine other reads  ·  17 Preview and place  ·  18 Replace and cancel  ·  19 What a schema cannot say
Chapter 15

The first tool, end to end

From a capability row to a passing test, with every decision shown. If you read one chapter of this book before writing a tool, read this one.

We are building brokerage_accounts_list: the tool that answers “what accounts do I have?”. It is the right first tool for a reason that is not obvious — it is the only tool in the catalog that consumes nothing, which makes it the only possible starting point for every conversation that touches a customer's money.

Step 1: the capability row

Before anything else, a row in the ontology. This is the design, and everything after it is implementation.

Four decisions are made in those six lines, and the build will hold us to all of them.

DecisionConsequence
operation: list Read-only and idempotent, by the ontology's own declaration. The annotations are now determined, not chosen.
entity: Account Classification floor customer-confidential, entitlement floor brokerage:accounts:read.
cardinality: many The plural term, so the name is accounts and not account.
consumes: [] No prerequisites. This tool appears in the generated briefing as a starting point and in the producer graph in column zero.

The name follows: brokerage + accounts + list. The risk tier follows from the operation: T0. The approval mode follows from the tier: none. None of those three is a judgment call now.

Step 2: the description

Write this before the schema. It is the field the model's choice turns on, and writing it first tends to expose that the tool is doing two things.

What it does. Returns every brokerage account the signed-in customer holds, with its identifier, nickname, type, currency and whether it can currently trade.

When to use it. Use when the customer mentions an account by nickname, refers to “my account” without saying which, or when any other brokerage tool needs an accountId and none is in hand yet — this is the only tool that needs nothing to run, so it is the safe first call.

When not to. Do not use to find out how much money is in an account; that is brokerage_balances_get.

How to read it. Read the type field before advising on anything: a CASH account cannot borrow, an IRA_TRADITIONAL or ROTH_IRA account cannot sell short, and any account whose tradeable field is false cannot place orders at all. Read restriction when tradeable is false and tell the customer the reason rather than retrying.

And the useful behavior. When the customer has more than one account and has not said which, ask; nickname and type together are usually enough for them to choose. This changes nothing and may be called freely.

982 characters. Notice how much of it is about the result rather than the call. That is the right proportion for a read tool: the call is trivial and the interpretation is where an agent goes wrong.

Step 3: the output schema

Also before the input schema, because what you return decides what the description had to say.

Three decisions worth naming.

tradeable is computed, not inferred

The restriction field already tells a model that FROZEN means no trading. The tradeable boolean says it again, as a certainty rather than an inference. The general rule: where a conclusion matters and is cheap to compute, compute it. A model is perfectly capable of working it out, and “perfectly capable” is a per-call probability.

The enum includes null

"enum": ["UNSETTLED_FUNDS", "DAY_TRADE_RESTRICTED", "FROZEN", null] with "type": ["string", "null"]. Null is a legitimate value — it means healthy — and leaving it out of the enum would make every healthy account fail the output validation the pipeline performs.

maxItems: 50

Nobody has fifty brokerage accounts. The bound is there because an unbounded array in a result is an unbounded token bill, and the one customer who has forty is a customer this tool should still work for.

Step 4: the input schema

One optional boolean. The interesting part is what is not here: there is no customerId. The customer is established by the runtime from the session, and the linter rejects the parameter by name. This is the single most important line of the chapter and it is a line that does not exist.

Step 5: the governance block

Every field here was decided in step 1 or is a fact about who maintains the tool. The tier, the approval mode and the entitlement all come from the ontology and are checked against it.

Step 6: the handler

And now the code, which is nineteen lines.

Read what it does not do. It does not validate arguments — the pipeline did. It does not check entitlements — the pipeline did. It does not catch exceptions, wrap a result, write an audit record or format an error. It takes the customer from the principal, maps four fields, and stops.

The handler-length heuristic. If a handler is long, it is usually because the tool is doing two things, and the fix is two tools. The second most common reason is that it is re-validating arguments the pipeline already validated — which means somebody did not trust the schema, and an untrusted schema is a schema the model is also being misled by.

Step 7: register it

There is no registration step. The handler is a Spring component, the descriptor is a file, and the registry matches them by name at startup. If either exists without the other the application does not start:

Step 8: the test

Two tests, and neither of them re-checks the schema — the pipeline already validated the payload against the descriptor's own output schema before the test saw it. What these assert are the claims the description makes.

And the one that matters more, which is about an account the customer does not hold:

NOT_FOUND and not NOT_ENTITLED. An authorization error tells the caller the account exists and belongs to somebody else; a not-found error tells them nothing. Since an agent cannot act on either, there is no cost to the uninformative answer and a real cost to the informative one — an enumeration oracle, driven by a model that will happily try a hundred identifiers if a prompt suggests it.

Step 9: run it

Nine steps, one of which was writing nineteen lines of Java. That proportion is the point of the whole book: in a well-built catalog the code is the small part, and the artifact that needs care is the contract.

Chapter 16

The nine other reads

Nine more tools, and eight ideas worth stealing.

The remaining read tools are variations on chapter 15, so rather than walking each one this chapter takes the design decision each exists to demonstrate.

1. Batch, and name it plural

brokerage_quotes_get takes up to ten symbols. An agent comparing three holdings will call a singular quote tool three times, and three round trips cost three times the latency, three audit records and three opportunities for one to fail on its own.

Batching is the cheapest performance decision in a catalog and it is made in the descriptor rather than the handler: the parameter is an array, the cardinality in the ontology is many, and the name is therefore plural. The description then has to say it out loud, because a model will otherwise do the obvious thing: “Pass every symbol in one call rather than calling once per symbol.”

There is an evaluation scenario that asserts exactly this, and it is the one that would catch a regression if somebody split the tool.

2. Name what you could not do

The same tool returns an unresolved array. A tool that quietly drops the symbols it could not price leaves the agent to notice that it asked for three and got two, and it will not notice.

3. Refuse to choose

brokerage_instruments_search is the only tool here whose entire design is a refusal. It returns candidates and an exactMatch flag, and leaves the choosing to the agent, which will put it to the customer.

The temptation to choose is strong, because ninety percent of queries have an obvious answer and returning one row makes the agent's job easier. The ten percent is the problem: “buy me some Apple” has two plausible tickers, “buy Google” has two share classes, and an order is not reversible. A tool that silently resolves ambiguity has moved a decision from the customer to a ranking function, and nobody reviewed the ranking function.

When the query is unambiguous the tool says so, so the agent need not ask:

4. Compute what the model would have to

brokerage_price_history_get returns bars and also the period high, the period low and the total return. A model given 120 rows of OHLCV will read some of them and do arithmetic in its head, and the arithmetic it is most likely to get wrong is the one it is most likely to be asked for.

A rule worth generalizing

If a model will have to compute something from your payload, and the computation is deterministic, compute it yourself. Payload size and arithmetic error go down together.

The same idea appears in brokerage_positions_list, which carries portfolioWeight per holding. A question about concentration is then one tool call and no division.

5. Order the result

Positions come back largest first. This is not cosmetic: a model reads a list from the top, and a long list from the top only. Putting the largest holdings first means that whatever gets dropped from a truncated answer is the part that mattered least. Ordering a result is the cheapest form of prioritization a tool has.

6. Default to the question that gets asked

brokerage_orders_list defaults state to WORKING. “Do I have any orders open?” is the question nine times in ten, and a tool whose default is six months of history makes the model pay for the other one and then summarize the wrong thing.

Defaults in a tool schema are not conveniences. They are the behavior you get, because a model omits an optional parameter far more often than it sets one. brokerage_executions_list makes the same decision with a 30-day window.

7. Cursors, never page numbers

The order book moves while the agent reads it. Page two of an offset-paginated list can repeat a row or skip one, and the agent will report whatever it was handed.

Two properties matter. The cursor is opaque, so moving to a keyset cursor over (placedAt, orderId) later is a day no caller has to change. And a malformed cursor is an INVALID_ARGUMENT rather than a silent reset to the first page — because silently starting over means an agent paging through a long list can loop forever, each time reporting the same first page as new.

8. Say when the answer does not apply

brokerage_tax_lots_list returns a taxable flag. In a retirement account none of the holding-period and wash-sale machinery means anything, and an agent that launches into a long-versus-short-term explanation inside a Roth IRA has wasted the customer's time and damaged their confidence in the whole system.

Rather than leaving the model to infer irrelevance from the account type, the tool says so.

What is deliberately absent

There is no brokerage_lots_select in this catalog. Choosing which tax lots to sell has consequences that outlive the conversation, and this firm's position is that a human instructs it. The agent's job is to put the choice in front of the customer, which it can only do if it can see the lots — so the read tool exists and the write tool does not.

That is a design pattern, not a gap. “Readable but not writable” is often the right answer for a capability that is genuinely useful and genuinely consequential. It gives the agent everything it needs to be helpful and nothing it needs to be dangerous, and it is a much easier conversation with a risk committee than “we built it with an approval step”.

Chapter 17

Preview and place

Two tools, one of which is read-only, and the mechanism that makes an agent physically unable to trade without pricing the trade first.

This is the design the rest of the catalog exists to support, so it is worth starting from the requirement rather than the solution.

The requirement

An order may be sent to the market only if (a) the exact terms were priced, (b) the customer was shown the price, (c) the customer agreed to those terms, and (d) a retry of the same approved instruction produces one order rather than two.

Three designs that do not work

A confirmed flag

brokerage_order_place(..., confirmed: true). A boolean the model sets is a boolean the model will eventually set — by a model that has convinced itself the customer already agreed three turns ago, which is a reasonable inference from a conversation and a catastrophic one from a control. The linter rejects the parameter name outright.

A dryRun flag

One tool, with dryRun: true meaning price it and false meaning do it. Better, in that the pricing and the placing cannot diverge. Worse in every other way: one tool means one description, one risk tier and one approval mode for two operations whose consequences differ by everything. Also rejected by name.

A rule in the system prompt

“Always call preview before place.” This one actually works most of the time, which is what makes it dangerous. It is a convention, enforced by the model's cooperation, and the conversations where it fails are the conversations where something unusual happened — which is also when you least want it to fail.

The design that does
