Two tools and a single-use token.

  • brokerage_order_preview is read-only, tier 1. It computes everything about the order and places nothing. When the order would be accepted, it issues a ConfirmationToken.
  • brokerage_order_place is tier 3 and requires a token.
  • Exactly one capability in the catalog produces a token, and it is the preview.

The agent cannot skip the preview because the argument does not exist anywhere else. That is a structural property, not a behavioral one, and it is checked by a test rather than hoped for.

What the token is bound to

A fingerprint of the exact ticket, the session it was issued to, and an expiry. All three earn their place:

Bound toStops
the fingerprint Placing 500 shares on a token minted for 50. Any change — quantity, price, side, time in force, account — is a different order and needs a new preview.
the session A token leaking between conversations, or a token from a transcript being replayed.
the expiry An order placed at a price the customer agreed to twenty minutes ago. Two minutes is long enough to read a summary and say yes, and short enough that the price is still roughly the price.

And it is single use, which is where the idempotency comes from.

Every refusal path returns a Rejection rather than throwing, because each one is something the agent can act on and the customer can be told — and the five are genuinely different. “That was already used” and “that is not the order you priced” need different next moves.

The preview

The preview's job is to compute everything the customer needs in order to agree, and to be honest about what would stop the order.

canPlace first, as the description instructs. Then the estimate, with isEstimate: true because a market order's fill is not knowable in advance. Then the token and its expiry.

Blockers and warnings are different things

This is the most load-bearing distinction in the risk engine. A blocker means the order would be refused: the agent must not proceed, and the right move is to tell the customer why. A warning means the order would go through but the customer may not want it to.

Collapsing them into one list of “issues” produces an agent that either ignores real refusals or refuses to place anything at all.

Two blockers, and they are not the same problem. One is a per-order notional ceiling; the other is that the account does not have the money. Each carries a maxPermissibleQuantity, which turns a dead end into an offer: the agent can say “the most this account could buy is 17 shares — would you like that?” instead of “I can't do that”.

Make a refusal actionable. When a tool refuses because of a limit, it almost always knows what would have been allowed. Returning that number costs nothing and is the difference between an agent that helps and an agent that reports.

And when the blocker is not about size, the field is explicitly null, so the agent does not offer a smaller version of something that is categorically disallowed:

No token when it cannot be placed

confirmationToken is null whenever canPlace is false. A refused order has nothing to approve, and handing back a token “just in case” would let an agent carry authority past the reason it was refused.

The place

Read the order of operations, because it is the whole design.

  1. The token is redeemed before the order is sent. Redeeming it is what proves these exact terms were priced and approved.
  2. A spent token is answered with the original order. Not an error — a retry is recognizably the same call, and duplicateOfPreviousCall tells the agent so in a field it cannot misread.
  3. The risk check runs again. Two minutes have passed and the market has moved. A preview is a promise about the moment it was taken, not a license.
  4. The idempotency key is derived from the token, not supplied by the model.

That last point is one line with a large consequence.

A model asked to supply a unique key will sometimes reuse one and sometimes invent a new one on a retry, and either failure mode defeats the guarantee. Deriving it from a single-use token means the guarantee does not depend on the model at all.

The whole chain, captured

Here is what the agent sees at each step, from the running system.

One. It calls place with a valid token, and the approval gate stops it:

Two. The customer is shown this, and says yes:

Three. The agent calls again, byte for byte, and the order goes:

Four. The agent, unsure whether that went through, retries:

One order. The same identifier. And a field that tells the agent to describe one order rather than two, which is the part a customer would otherwise notice.

The token and the approval are two mechanisms

A fair question at this point: if the customer has to approve at the gate anyway, why is there also a token?

Because they guarantee different things, and each is useless alone.

MechanismGuaranteesDoes not guarantee
The token The terms were priced, by this service, moments ago, and have not changed since. And that a retry is not a second order. That any human was involved.
The approval gate A human was shown a summary and said yes to these arguments in this session. That the summary was true, or that anything priced it.

Together they give you: a human agreed to a priced instruction that had not changed, and it happened once. There is a test for each half, and chapter 22 is about the gate.

Chapter 18

Replace and cancel

Two tools that change something, and the asymmetry between them that is worth defending out loud.

Replace is tier 3, like placing

This is the one people push back on, so here is the argument in one sentence: raising a limit from 495 to 512 and buying at 512 are the same economic act. The customer's exposure changes by exactly the same amount either way.

A catalog that treats amendment as a lesser operation has given the agent a cheaper route to the same outcome, and cheaper routes get used. So replace needs the same approval, the same confirmation token, and the same evidence as place.

The order keeps its identifier

A customer who was told “your order number is ord_CZ9R...” and then hears about ord_7K2M has lost the thread, and an agent asked to “move my limit up a dollar” has no business creating a second order. So an amendment is in place.

Some fields an amendment cannot change

Quantity, limit price and stop price are amendable. Side, order type and time in force are not: they are properties of the order, and a request to change one is a request to cancel and re-enter. The handler takes them from the order rather than from the arguments, and a conflicting argument is an error rather than a silent reinterpretation.

That method is also what keeps the fingerprint honest, and the comment explains a bug this book actually had: when the preview took the time in force from the arguments rather than from the order, previewing an amendment to a good-till-canceled order minted a token the replace tool could never spend. The failure surfaced as “the order does not match the one that was confirmed” — which is true, and completely unhelpful.

Cancel is tier 2, and needs no token

The one asymmetry in the catalog. Cancelling reduces exposure. Requiring a priced preview before a customer can stop an order would mean that in the one situation where speed matters — a price running away from them — the system is at its slowest.

A human still approves the call. What it does not need is a round trip through the risk engine to find out what stopping something would cost.

The race, reported honestly

This is the part of the cancel tool that justifies its existence as a separate chapter. An order can fill in the moment between the customer asking and the venue hearing. When that happens:

Read the envelope. ok is true. Nothing failed: the call worked, and the answer is that the order filled. cancelled is false, status is FILLED, and explanation says it in words the agent can read aloud.

Returning an error here would be wrong twice over. Nothing failed, and an agent that sees an error will retry — which in this case means asking the venue to cancel an order that no longer exists, repeatedly, while telling the customer nothing.

The failure this prevents is specific. An agent that says “I've canceled that for you” about an order that filled leaves a customer who believes they are flat and is not. They find out at the next statement, or when the position moves against them. It is the single most expensive thing a well-meaning agent can say.

The contrast is worth seeing side by side — the same tool, on an order that was still working:

Same shape, different values, and the agent branches on cancelled rather than on the absence of an error. The description tells it to: “Read cancelled and status together rather than assuming success.”

Partial fills

On a partially filled order the shares that already filled remain, and only the unfilled remainder is canceled. The explanation says so, with the numbers, because reporting the order as CANCELLED on an order that was half done is another way to leave a customer with a position they do not know about.

Repeating a cancellation is harmless

Calling cancel on an already canceled order reports the same final state and does nothing. The description says so, which matters because an agent that is unsure whether its cancellation landed should feel free to check, and the cheapest way to check is to ask again.

Chapter 19

What a schema cannot say

Cross-field rules, and where to put them so that the model still learns them.

“A limit price is required when the order type is LIMIT” is expressible in JSON Schema. It is a conditional, and conditionals are banned by the profile in chapter 7. This chapter is the bill for that decision, and the argument that it is worth paying.

Why the conditional is not an option

Most tool-calling runtimes drop if/then on the way to the model. So the model is shown a schema in which limitPrice is simply optional, produces a LIMIT order without one, and the handler has to catch it anyway. You have written the rule twice — once in a schema the model never saw, once in the handler — and the schema is now a document that lies.

The trade

State a cross-field rule in the description, where the model reads it, and enforce it in the handler, where a violation becomes an error the model can act on. That is two places. The alternative is also two places, plus a schema that disagrees with both.

Where the rules live

Four lines of rule-checking, each covering a pair of order types, and each producing an error that names the field and says what to do:

Note the remediation: “Ask the customer what price they want and re-send with limitPrice set.” Not “provide limitPrice”. The agent's next move is a question to a human, and saying so is the difference between an agent that asks and an agent that invents a price.

The rules that are not about arguments at all

Most of what stops an order has nothing to do with the shape of the request. The risk engine checks nine things, and every one of them is about the state of the world rather than the contents of the ticket.

CheckProduces
sessionA blocker when the market is closed and the order would expire, or when a market order is entered outside the regular session. A warning otherwise in pre-market and after-hours.
permissionsBlockers for a frozen account, a short sale in a cash or retirement account, a non-marginable instrument bought on margin, a day-trade restriction.
sizeA share ceiling and a notional ceiling, each with the size that would have been allowed.
fundingBuying power in a margin account, settled cash in a cash account — which is why the balances tool returns both.
inventorySelling more than is held, which is a short sale and must be entered as one deliberately.
pricingA blocker at more than 30 percent from the market, a warning at more than 10. The first is a mistyped-price guard; the second is a “this will sit unfilled” guard.
concentrationA warning above 25 percent of the account.
taxesWarnings about wash-sale exposure and mixed holding periods, suppressed entirely in a retirement account.

One detail worth stealing

The concentration check only runs when there are no blockers.

Without that guard, an order for four thousand shares in an account that cannot afford forty produces the warning “MSFT would be 6,794 percent of the account”. It is arithmetically true and it is noise, and noise in a warnings array is how an agent learns to skim it.

And the rules that are about the account, not the order

A frozen account is refused before anything is priced, by a guard every handler that takes an account calls:

“Do not try another account on their behalf.” That clause is in the remediation because the obvious helpful thing to do with a frozen account is to suggest a different one, and the obvious helpful thing is wrong: the customer said which account, and an agent that moves an order somewhere else has substituted its judgment for theirs on a question about money.

Part V

The registry
and the runtime

Everything that happens around a handler: what exists, who may call it, in what order the checks run, where a human says yes, and how the whole thing is published to Spring AI in one class.

20 The registry  ·  21 The invocation pipeline  ·  22 Approval, limits and switches  ·  23 The audit record  ·  24 Publishing to Spring AI
Chapter 20

The registry

It sounds like plumbing and it is in fact the main architectural decision in a tool system.

Without a registry, the set of tools a model sees is whatever beans happened to be on the classpath. That sounds harmless until somebody asks one of these four questions, all of which get asked:

  1. What is the model being shown right now?
  2. Who is allowed to call each of these?
  3. Which of them have been reviewed?
  4. What breaks if we turn one off?

With a registry, all four are lookups.

Three rules, enforced at construction

Deliberately early, so that a misconfigured catalog fails at startup rather than in a conversation.

Every descriptor has a handler and every handler has a descriptor
A handler with no descriptor is dead code. A descriptor with no handler is worse: a tool the model will choose and then be told does not work, which costs a turn and teaches it nothing.
Every descriptor passes the conformance linter
A registry that serves a non-conformant descriptor has made the specification advisory. The findings are kept, so the console can show a reviewer what the gate saw, but any error stops the application.
Only active tools are served
Draft and retired tools are skipped, however complete they look. The lifecycle field is the switch between “this exists in the repository” and “a model can call this”, and those should not be the same thing.

The selection view

The registry's most-used method is one line, and the reasoning behind it is the whole chapter.

Filtering before publication rather than refusing at execution is not an optimization. A tool the principal cannot use, published into the model's context, costs tokens on every turn and buys a wrong turn: the model will choose it, be refused, apologize, and choose again. Showing a model only what it can do is the cheapest accuracy improvement available.

One catalog, three products

The same fourteen descriptors, the same handlers and the same pipeline, published to three sessions that differ only in their entitlements.

RoleTools Sees
RESEARCH3 instruments_search, quotes_get, price_history_get
SERVICE10 the three above, plus accounts_list, balances_get, positions_list, tax_lots_list, orders_list, order_get, executions_list
TRADING14 all of the above, plus order_preview, order_place, order_replace, order_cancel

Nothing is reconfigured to make that happen, and no tool is rewritten. There is an HTTP test that asserts the three counts, because the day one of them changes silently is the day a research session can read a customer's balances.

And what is hidden, for the humans

The registry can also answer the inverse question — which tools this principal cannot see, and which scope is missing. That is never shown to the model; it is for the console, and for the support engineer wondering why the agent said it could not do something.

Chapter 21

The invocation pipeline

Ten steps, in an order that is argued for rather than assumed. This is the system.

A handler is domain code. The pipeline is the part that makes a tool catalog safe to point a language model at, and it is identical for all fourteen tools — which is precisely why it belongs in one place and not in any of them.

Steps 1 and 2: resolve, and check the switch

Note that an unknown name and a name this principal cannot see produce the same error. Telling the model “that tool exists but is off limits” is an oracle it will probe, and since it cannot act on either answer there is no cost to the uninformative one.

Steps 3 and 4: parse and validate

The remediation is as important as the message. “Fix the fields named above and call the tool again. Do not try a different tool.” An agent that reads an argument error as “this tool does not work” will go looking for another one, and the other one will have the same problem.

Step 5 after step 4, which looks backwards

Arguments are validated before entitlements are checked. For a human-facing API that is the wrong order: you refuse the unauthorized caller first and tell them nothing else.

For a model it is the wrong order for a different reason. The useful answer to a malformed call is “your third argument is wrong”, and giving it a bare NOT_ENTITLED teaches it to retry the same malformed call against a different tool. Nothing leaks, because the tool was already in this principal's visible catalog before the pipeline ran — step 1 saw to that.

The general form

Information is withheld at the point where visibility is decided, not at the point where a call is refused. Once a tool is visible to a session, that session may learn everything about how to call it correctly.

Step 6: the rate limit

Rate limiting a tool catalog is not about load. It is about the one failure mode a language model has that a human caller does not: a loop. An agent that misreads an error as transient will retry it, politely, for as many turns as the budget allows.

The limit is per tool, not per catalog, because the limits that matter differ by two orders of magnitude. And the error carries the wait, because “too many requests” with no number means the agent waits zero seconds.

Step 7: the approval gate

Chapter 22 is about the gate itself. What matters here is where it sits: after validation, after entitlement, after the rate limit, and before the handler. A human is asked about a call that is already known to be well-formed and permitted, which is the only kind of call it is reasonable to ask a human about.

Step 8: the handler runs

And only now. Note what the handler is given.

A descriptor, validated arguments, a principal and a request identifier. Note what is not there: the conversation. A handler cannot read the chat history, cannot see the system prompt, and cannot be talked into anything, because it is never shown the talking. That is the whole reason a tool is a safer surface than a prompt.

Step 9: verify the payload

This is the step people leave out, and the one worth the most argument.

Validating your own handler's output sounds like distrust of your colleagues. It is distrust of drift. The output schema is the only description of the payload the model will ever see. The day a handler adds a field, renames one, or starts returning null where it used to return a number, the model is being misled by a document the firm published — and nothing else in the system will notice.

Failing closed turns that into a caught bug with a request identifier, rather than a confusing conversation three weeks later. The error returned to the model carries no detail at all, because the model cannot act on it and a customer should not read it.

Step 10: envelope and audit

And the two things that happen on every path, successful or not.

Everything a handler may throw

Exactly one thing, and the pipeline catches the rest.

A ToolFailure becomes the envelope the handler intended. Anything else is logged with the request identifier and returned as INTERNAL_ERROR with no detail — because the alternative is a database constraint name in a customer conversation, and there is a test asserting it does not happen.

What this buys, in one table

Without the pipelineWith it
Each handler validates, or does not Every call validated against the published schema, once, in one place
Entitlements checked where somebody remembered Checked for every tool, from the descriptor's own declaration
Approval is a convention in the prompt A gate the model cannot route around, keyed to the exact arguments
Errors are whatever the handler threw Fifteen codes, each with a next action the agent was taught
Audit is where somebody added a log line Every invocation, written before the handler and completed after
A drifting handler misleads the model quietly A drifting handler fails the call and names the request
Chapter 22

Approval, limits and switches

Where a human says yes, how to stop a loop, and how to turn a tool off at two in the morning.

The approval gate

The mechanism is a reference rather than a flag, and that distinction is the whole design. A flag can be set by the thing being checked. A reference is a hash of the tool name, the exact arguments and the session.

Canonical JSON, so that a re-ordered argument object is still the same approval and a changed value is not. An approval granted for “buy 50 AAPL at market” cannot be spent on “buy 500”, and an approval from one conversation cannot be spent in another.

Three steps, and it survives a restart

  1. The agent calls a tool that needs approval. The gate has no grant for that reference, so the pipeline returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED with the reference and a rendered summary of what is about to happen.
  2. Something outside the model shows the summary to a human and records their answer against the reference. In this repository that is the Angular console; in production it is whatever surface the customer is actually on.
  3. The agent calls the tool again, byte for byte. Now the grant matches and it runs.

Nothing about that flow requires the agent process to be the same one, or even to be running, between steps 1 and 3.

Grants are single use and they expire

An approval with no window is a standing instruction, and nobody means to give one of those. There are three tests, and between them they say the whole thing:

The dialog, and the context behind it

Chapter 9 made the case; here is the mechanism. The template is rendered from the arguments plus whatever the domain supplies, and the domain's values win.

An unresolved placeholder is left visible as (not given) rather than blanked, because a dialog with a quietly empty field is how somebody approves an order whose quantity they never saw. And the brokerage's own context re-prices the order at the moment of the confirmation:

If the order can no longer be placed at all, the dialog says so instead of quoting a cost. A confirmation prompt for an order that would be refused is worse than useless: the customer says yes, the tool refuses, and they have learned that the approval step is theatre.

Rate limits

A sliding window per principal and per tool. The numbers in this catalog range from 180 a minute for quotes to 10 a minute for placing an order, and the ratio is the point: a tool that is cheap and idempotent should be generous, and a tool that spends money should not.

Kill switches

Every tool at tier 2 or above must name one, and the linter enforces it. The reason only becomes obvious the first time you need it: when a tool starts behaving badly at two in the morning, the options are to turn it off or to roll back, and only one of those takes less than a build.

Switches are hierarchical by prefix, so tools.brokerage.trading disables tools.brokerage.trading.place and its siblings with it. That matters when the thing misbehaving is a dependency rather than a tool.

And the effect on the agent is the point: a tripped switch does not produce an error the agent will retry. The tool leaves the catalog on the next turn, so the model does not see it at all.

Chapter 23

The audit record

What to write, what never to write, and why it is written twice.

Written before, completed after

A record is written before the handler runs and completed after, so that a call which hangs or crashes the process still leaves evidence it was attempted. Logging on the way out loses exactly the invocations an incident review cares about.

What is deliberately absent

Arguments are recorded as a hash and a list of field names, never as values.

The reasoning: the record has to prove which call was made and let a reviewer match it against an approval, and a hash does both. Storing the values themselves would put account identifiers, order sizes and whatever the customer typed into a log with a six-year retention and a much wider readership than the account itself.

What an incident review actually needs

Here is the trail left by the preview-then-place sequence from chapter 17.

Four things an auditor can do with that, none of which require the application to be running:

  • Join the action to the approval. Both place records carry the same approval reference; one is the request and one is the execution.
  • Prove the order of operations. The preview preceded the place, and the timestamps say by how long.
  • Know the retention and the basis. Each record carries its own, from the descriptor, so a record does not have to be joined to a catalog that may have changed.
  • Find the conversation. The session identifier, and the request identifier the customer was given if they complained.

There is a test for the first of those, because it is the one that matters and the one a refactor would silently break.

In production

This implementation keeps the last few thousand records in memory so the console can show them and the tests can assert on them. In a real firm it writes to the immutable store, and the interesting design question is not where but what else: the audit record is the only artifact that survives the conversation, so anything you will want to ask later has to be in it now.

One field worth adding that this implementation does not have. The model and model version that made the call. When selection accuracy moves after a model upgrade, the first question is which calls were made by which version, and the only place that can be answered is here.

Chapter 24

Publishing to Spring AI

The whole binding, in one class, with no annotations anywhere.

Everything in this book so far has been about a contract that names no framework. This is where it meets one, and the measure of whether the preceding chapters were right is how little code this takes.

Spring AI wants three strings per tool: a name, a description and a serialized input schema. The descriptor has all three, so the adapter reads them off and hands them over. There is no translation, no mapping table and no annotation processor.

What the callback deliberately does not do

It hands the raw argument string to the pipeline and returns whatever JSON comes back. It does not validate, authorize, catch or format — because doing any of those here would mean they happened only for callers who came through Spring AI, and the desktop connector and the test harness would each need their own copy.

Contrast with the annotated approach

Spring AI supports @Tool on a method, which is the obvious thing to reach for and is faster for the first three tools. Here is what it costs at fourteen.

 @Tool on a methodA descriptor file
The description A string literal in a Java file. Nobody lints it; a reviewer reading the diff is reading Java. Prose in a file, linted against ten rules, and a diff a product owner can read.
The input schema Inferred from parameter types. You get the types; you do not get patterns, enums, bounds or per-property descriptions without more annotations. Written explicitly, and checked against a profile.
Seeing what the model gets Start the application and inspect. cat the file.
Publishing elsewhere Another framework's annotations, or a reflection pass. An adapter of about forty lines that renames nothing.
Governance Nowhere obvious. Usually a spreadsheet. In the file, next to the thing it governs.

Publishing per turn, not per application

Each call builds fresh callbacks bound to this session's principal and to a fresh trace. Two consequences follow: a research session and a trading session running at the same moment see different catalogs, and every turn comes back with a complete record of what was called.

The agent

There is no hand-rolled tool-call loop. Spring AI runs it, because there is nothing to gain from driving it manually: the trace is collected inside each callback, so the visibility a manual loop is usually written for is already there. Less machinery, same evidence.

The trace

Which brings us to the most useful artifact in the whole system, and the one that is almost always missing.

When an agent gives a wrong answer, the question is never “what did the model say” — you have that. It is “which tools did it call, with what arguments, in what order, and what came back”. Without a trace you are reduced to reading the final prose and guessing.

The trace is also what makes the test harness possible. Selection accuracy, argument accuracy and trajectory assertions are all statements about this list, so the harness becomes a set of expectations over a trace rather than a set of expectations over English. Part VII is about that.

The agent
